section.title: A Lament for Egypt
section.sectionRationale: This chapter widens the scope of Egypt's judgment to include her allies and pictures a day of the LORD falling on Egypt and everyone who depends on her, naming city after city that will burn or fall by the sword, before closing with a second oracle in which Pharaoh's arm, once raised in strength, is shown already broken and about to be broken further, while Babylon's arm is strengthened in its place.
section.thesis: The day of the LORD comes not only for Israel but for every nation and every ally bound up with a proud power like Egypt, whose broken arm no human effort can heal, showing that trust placed in any strength but God's own is trust placed in something already failing.
section.frameNote: Two oracles: a wide ranging lament naming Egypt's allies and cities in turn as the day of the LORD falls upon them all; and a second, later oracle picturing Pharaoh's arm already broken, soon to be shattered entirely while the LORD strengthens the arm of Babylon's king in its place.

units.label: The day of the LORD is near
units.note: for Egypt and all her helpers

verses.text: Again the word of the LORD came to me, saying,
“Son of man, prophesy and declare that this is what the Lord GOD says: Wail, 'Alas for that day!'
For the day is near, the {{yom-yhwh|Day of the LORD}} is near. It will be a day of clouds, a time of doom for the nations.
A sword will come against Egypt, and there will be anguish in Cush when the slain fall in Egypt, its wealth is taken away, and its foundations are torn down.
Cush, Put, and Lud, and all the various peoples, as well as Libya and the men of the covenant land, will fall with Egypt by the sword.
For this is what the LORD says: The allies of Egypt will fall, and her proud strength will collapse. From Migdol to Syene they will fall by the sword within her, declares the Lord GOD.
They will be desolate among desolate lands, and their cities will lie among ruined cities.
Then they will know that I am the LORD when I set fire to Egypt and all her helpers are shattered.
On that day messengers will go out from Me in ships to frighten Cush out of complacency. Anguish will come upon them on the day of Egypt's doom. For it is indeed coming.
This is what the Lord GOD says: I will put an end to the hordes of Egypt by the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon.
He and his people with him, the most ruthless of the nations, will be brought in to destroy the land. They will draw their swords against Egypt and fill the land with the slain.
I will make the streams dry up and sell the land to the wicked. By the hands of foreigners I will bring desolation upon the land and everything in it. I, the LORD, have spoken.

units.label: City after city named
units.note: Memphis, Zoan, Thebes, and the rest

verses.text: This is what the Lord GOD says: I will destroy the idols and put an end to the images in Memphis. There will no longer be a prince in Egypt, and I will instill fear in that land.
I will lay waste Pathros, set fire to Zoan, and execute judgment on Thebes.
I will pour out My wrath on Pelusium, the stronghold of Egypt, and cut off the crowds of Thebes.
I will set fire to Egypt, Pelusium will writhe in anguish, Thebes will be split open, and Memphis will face daily distress.
The young men of On and Pi-beseth will fall by the sword, and those cities will go into captivity.
The day will be darkened in Tahpanhes when I break the yoke of Egypt and her proud strength comes to an end. A cloud will cover her, and her daughters will go into captivity.
So I will execute judgment on Egypt, and they will know that I am the LORD.”
In the eleventh year, on the seventh day of the first month, the word of the LORD came to me, saying,
“Son of man, I have broken the {{zroa|arm}} of Pharaoh king of Egypt. See, it has not been bound up for healing, or splinted for strength to hold the sword.

Therefore this is what the Lord GOD says: Behold, I am against Pharaoh king of Egypt. I will break his arms, both the strong one and the one already broken, and will make the sword fall from his hand.
I will disperse the Egyptians among the nations and scatter them throughout the lands.
I will strengthen the arms of Babylon's king and place My sword in his hand, but I will break the arms of Pharaoh, who will groan before him like a mortally wounded man.

I will strengthen the arms of Babylon's king, but Pharaoh's arms will fall limp. Then they will know that I am the LORD, when I place My sword in the hand of Babylon's king, and he wields it against the land of Egypt.
I will disperse the Egyptians among the nations and scatter them throughout the lands. Then they will know that I am the LORD.”

yom-yhwh.gloss: The Day of the LORD, a recurring prophetic phrase for a decisive moment when God intervenes in judgment or salvation, most often associated with Israel's own accountability but here, strikingly, applied to Egypt and the nations, showing that this day belongs to every people, not Israel alone.

zroa.gloss: The arm, a common biblical picture of strength, especially military power, as in 'the arm of the LORD' or 'the arm of flesh.' Pharaoh's arm, once a symbol of Egypt's might, is declared already broken and beyond human healing, while the LORD strengthens Babylon's arm in its place.

basic.context: This chapter widens the scope of Egypt's judgment from the previous chapter's focus on Pharaoh himself to include Egypt's regional allies, Cush, Put, Lud, Libya, and names city after city across Egypt, Memphis, Zoan, Thebes, Pelusium, and more, that will fall in the coming devastation, before a second, later oracle pictures Pharaoh's arm as already broken beyond human healing while the LORD deliberately strengthens the arm of Babylon's king against him.
basic.hermeneutics: This describes a real, historically anchored judgment on Egypt and her actual regional allies and cities, most of which are identifiable ancient Egyptian centers, fulfilled substantially through Babylonian incursions into Egypt in the following decades. The 'Day of the LORD' language, elsewhere often tied to Israel's own accountability, here describes God's real, historical intervention against Egypt specifically, while also carrying the wider prophetic resonance this phrase always holds of God's ultimate reckoning with all nations.
basic.originalLanguages: This is called the yom YHWH, the Day of the LORD, language usually reserved for Israel's own accountability but here turned outward to Egypt, showing that this decisive day belongs to every nation. And Pharaoh's zeroa, his arm, the biblical symbol of military strength, is declared already broken beyond human splinting, while God deliberately strengthens Babylon's arm to wield the sword against him.
basic.typology: Pharaoh's broken arm, beyond any human splint or bandage to heal, anticipates the wider biblical truth that human strength, 'the arm of flesh,' always fails, while only 'the arm of the LORD' truly saves, a phrase Isaiah later applies directly to the coming Messiah, Isaiah 53:1.
basic.christ: Where Pharaoh's arm is broken and cannot be healed by any human effort, Isaiah later asks 'to whom has the arm of the LORD been revealed', Isaiah 53:1, answered in Christ, the true and only arm of salvation, whose strength, unlike Pharaoh's, cannot be broken and needs no human splint to hold it.
basic.god: God is Lord of history, deliberately breaking one nation's power while deliberately strengthening another's, even a pagan empire like Babylon, entirely for His own purposes; His sovereignty is not passive but active, personally breaking Pharaoh's arms and personally placing His own sword in Nebuchadnezzar's hand.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 19:1-25 and Jeremiah 46:1-26 give companion oracles against Egypt from the same general period. Isaiah 53:1 asks 'to whom has the arm of the LORD been revealed', a phrase this chapter's broken 'arm of Pharaoh' sets in sharp relief. Joel 2:1-2 and Zephaniah 1:14-15 use similar 'day of clouds' and 'Day of the LORD' language for coming judgment on nations generally.
basic.oneStory: Egypt's proud strength and all her allies fall on the day the LORD Himself declares, her king's arm broken beyond human healing while Babylon's arm is strengthened for God's own purposes. This anticipates the whole biblical truth that every human arm of strength eventually fails, while the true arm of the LORD, revealed fully in Christ, alone accomplishes a salvation that cannot be broken.

context.literary:
The chapter is a diptych. The first half, verses 1 to 19, is a poem that opens with a command to wail and then works outward in widening rings: the day itself in verses 2 to 4, the allies in verses 5 to 9, Babylon as the sword in verses 10 to 12, and then a litany of Egyptian cities in verses 13 to 18. The second half, verses 20 to 26, is a separate dated oracle, in prose, about a single arm. The two panels are bound by the closing formula 'Then they will know that I am the LORD,' verses 8, 19, 25 and 26.

The poem is shaped like a map being unrolled. It begins in the sky, with a day of clouds, moves to the borders, 'From Migdol to Syene,' verse 6, and then drops down the Nile from the delta to the south: Memphis, Pathros, Zoan, Thebes, Pelusium, On, Pi-beseth, Tahpanhes, verses 13 to 18. The effect is a sweep of judgment that touches every part of the country, and the repeated fire and sword turn a list of places into a drumbeat.

The second panel changes imagery completely. In place of the sky and the cities there is one body part, the arm, and a small drama of medicine: an arm broken, not bound up, not splinted, verse 21, and then a second break promised, verse 22, with God as both surgeon and strong man. The word 'sword' ties the halves together, since the sword falls from Pharaoh's hand in verse 22 and is placed in Babylon's hand in verses 24 and 25.
context.historical:
The first poem is undated, but verse 20 fixes the second oracle to the eleventh year, first month, seventh day, which is the spring of 587 BC by the usual reckoning, while Jerusalem was still under siege. The break of Pharaoh's arm may refer to the Egyptian army's failed attempt to relieve the city, which Jeremiah 37:5 to 8 describes: Pharaoh's army came out, the Babylonians withdrew, and then returned. An earlier break had come at Carchemish in the fourth year of Jehoiakim, Jeremiah 46:2, when Nebuchadnezzar defeated Neco's army on the Euphrates. Verse 22 speaks of 'both the strong one and the one already broken,' which fits a history of two blows.

The lists of peoples reflect Egypt's real military economy. Cush, Put and Lud, and 'all the various peoples,' were mercenary and allied contingents, and Jeremiah 46:9 speaks in a similar way of Cush and Put carrying shields and men of Lydia drawing the bow. Verse 5 adds Libya and 'the men of the covenant land,' a phrase whose meaning is uncertain. The cities cover the Nile from north to south. Memphis was the ancient capital, Zoan is Tanis in the delta, Pelusium guarded the eastern approach, Tahpanhes was a frontier fortress where Jeremiah 43:8 to 13 foretold that Nebuchadnezzar would set up his throne, and Thebes was the great religious centre of the south, the city of the god Amon, as Jeremiah 46:25 notes.

The 'messengers in ships' of verse 9 recall the couriers sent by sea in Isaiah 18:1 to 2, and suggest that the news of Egypt's collapse would rattle even far Cush.
context.canonical:
The 'Day of the LORD' began as a hope. Amos 5:18 had to correct Israelites who longed for it and who assumed it meant only trouble for their enemies. Isaiah 2:12 to 13 made it a day against all that is proud and lofty, even the cedars of Lebanon. Zephaniah 1:14 to 15 gives the same day a rich vocabulary, including a day of 'clouds and blackness,' which Ezekiel adopts with 'a day of clouds,' verse 3. Obadiah 15 says outright that the Day of the LORD is near 'for all the nations.' Ezekiel pulls this strand to the centre of an oracle against a foreign power.

The arm is another thread. God redeemed Israel from Egypt 'with an outstretched arm,' Exodus 6:6, and the Psalms pray for the arm of the wicked to be broken, Psalm 10:15. In Ezekiel 30 the old Exodus arm now falls on Egypt itself, and Pharaoh's arm is the one in splints. The idea of the helpless healer comes up again in Ezekiel 34:4, where failed shepherds have not 'bound up the injured.'

The New Testament inherits the day. Peter says at Pentecost that the sun will be turned to darkness before the coming of the great Day of the Lord, Acts 2:20, and Paul tells the Thessalonians that it will come like a thief, 1 Thessalonians 5:2. Peter also says the elements will be destroyed by fire, 2 Peter 3:10. Egypt's smaller day is a rehearsal for the larger one.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Ezekiel's hearers wanted to know whether Egypt could still save them. Chapter 29 had called Egypt a broken reed. Chapter 30 closes the door more firmly: the day is near, and it is not just for Pharaoh but for his whole coalition. 'Her allies will fall' is a statement that nobody who leans on Egypt will escape.

The second oracle seems aimed at the same hope in a more acute form. Pharaoh had suffered one setback and perhaps people said he would recover. The prophet answers with a doctor's report: the arm is broken, nobody has set it, and now the other arm is going too. The instruction to the exiles is practical: do not wait for a rescue from the south, and do not read Egypt's temporary advances as the turning of the tide. God has chosen the sword that will win, and it is a Babylonian one.

The repeated 'they will know that I am the LORD' also tells the exiles that the history they are living through is not random. The destruction of an empire is a message. Egypt's fall, like Judah's, was meant to reveal the God who had spoken, and the exiles themselves were included in that audience.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes God's judgment on a particular nation and the particular instruments He chose. It does not authorise anyone to treat their own enemy as the target of God's sword, and it does not make Babylon a model of righteousness. Jeremiah 51:20 calls Babylon God's war club, but Isaiah 10:5 to 6 and Jeremiah 25:12 make clear that the instrument is itself later judged. A reader should not conclude that God approves of every army He uses, or that military success is a sign of divine favour.

What the chapter does ask of later readers is a way of seeing. Strength that is not tied to God is already broken, whether it is a state, an alliance, a market or a reputation. The call to wail 'Alas for that day!' is also a call to take warnings about coming reckoning seriously, and not to assume they apply only to other people. The New Testament applies the Day of the Lord to everyone, 1 Thessalonians 5:2 to 3, and invites the same sober readiness.

debates.question: Who are 'the men of the covenant land' in verse 5?

views.label: Jewish mercenaries or refugees in Egypt
views.case: The Hebrew is literally 'the sons of the land of the covenant', and some read it as a reference to Israelites or Judeans who had gone to Egypt, as Jeremiah 44:1 describes Jews living in Migdol, Tahpanhes, Memphis and Pathros. They would then fall with the ally they chose.

views.label: Allies bound to Egypt by treaty
views.case: Others take 'covenant' in the sense of a political treaty, so that the phrase names a land allied with Egypt, perhaps a nearby people bound to her by oath. This fits the surrounding list of peoples bound together in military alliance.

views.label: An unknown ethnic name or an old textual problem
views.case: A third view holds that the phrase may be a corrupt or obscure name, perhaps another ally. The Greek translation takes it differently, and the BSB does not footnote it, so certainty is not available.

debates.bearing: Whichever is right, the verse says that the fall reaches everyone attached to Egypt. If the phrase does mean Judeans, then it deepens verse 16 of the previous chapter: trust in Egypt places the trusting in the path of the sword.

debates.question: What are the two arms of verse 22?

views.label: Two successive defeats
views.case: The arm already broken is the defeat at Carchemish in the time of Neco, Jeremiah 46:2, or the retreat of Pharaoh's army from Jerusalem, Jeremiah 37:5 to 8. The second break is the one still to come.

views.label: Strong arm and weak arm in the same king
views.case: The phrase 'both the strong one and the one already broken' can be read as a figure for the whole of Egypt's strength, healthy and wounded together, so that nothing is left, with no need to pin it to two specific events.

debates.bearing: Either way, the arm that held the sword is gone, and the verse insists that the cause is God's decision, not only military setback. A bandaged arm will not hold the sword again.

study.originalLanguages:
The command in verse 2 is 'Wail,' a word that belongs to the cry of mourners, and it is followed by 'Alas for that day,' a cry that sounds like the keening of a funeral. Isaiah 13:6 begins its own day-of-the-LORD oracle in the same register, 'Wail, for the Day of the LORD is near.' In Ezekiel the cry is aimed at a foreign land, and it is the prophet who is to lead it.

The 'Day of the LORD' of verse 3 is yom YHWH, and it is paired with the 'day of clouds,' using anan, the ordinary Hebrew word for cloud. In Zephaniah 1:15 the same day is 'a day of clouds and blackness.' A footnote notes that the Hebrew of verse 3 has no 'of doom,' so the text reads simply 'a time for the nations,' which makes the phrase a bare, ominous statement of timing: it is the nations' time.

The 'proud strength' of verses 6 and 18 is ga'on, a word for pride, pomp or swelling dignity, and the word for 'strength' is oz. The phrase says that Egypt's honour and might are one thing and fall together. In verse 18 the day is 'darkened' in Tahpanhes when God 'breaks the yoke of Egypt.' The yoke of Egypt had once meant slavery for Israel, Leviticus 26:13 and Exodus 6:6, and now it is Egypt's own yoke that is broken.

The arm of verses 21 to 25 is zeroa, the standard Hebrew word for the arm as the seat of strength. It is the same word as the 'outstretched arm' of the Exodus in Exodus 6:6. Verse 21 uses the vocabulary of the doctor's bench: the arm has not been 'bound up,' from chavash, the verb of wrapping a wound, which Ezekiel 34:4 uses of what the shepherds failed to do for the injured. What began as a metaphor of military strength is now cast in terms of a wound that no one has tended.

The verbs for what God does with the two arms are mirror images: He 'breaks' Pharaoh's and 'strengthens' Babylon's, and in the same breath He 'places My sword in his hand,' verses 24 and 25. The sword is God's, the hand is Babylon's. The English 'fall limp' of verse 25 is a literal falling, the arms dropping, and the 'groan' of verse 24 is the cry of a wounded man, nothing like the roar of a champion.

typology.type: The Day of the LORD against Egypt, Ezekiel 30:2 to 4
typology.fulfillment: A near day, with a sword, clouds and anguish, is a small preview of the great day. Jesus uses the darkened sun and moon for the coming of the Son of Man, Matthew 24:29, and Peter at Pentecost speaks of the sun turned to darkness before the great and glorious Day of the Lord, Acts 2:20. Egypt's day is real, but it is a type: the final Day of the Lord will come like a thief, 1 Thessalonians 5:2, and will lay the earth and its works bare, 2 Peter 3:10. The type falls short because Egypt's day ends in a land that is eventually inhabited again, Jeremiah 46:26, while the final day ends in a new heaven and a new earth.

typology.type: Pharaoh's broken arm that no one bandages, Ezekiel 30:21
typology.fulfillment: The wound that has not been bound up and cannot hold a sword points to every human strength that cannot be mended. Isaiah 59:16 and 63:5 see no human helper and say 'His own arm brought salvation.' Mary sings that God 'has performed mighty deeds with His arm,' Luke 1:51. In Christ the divine arm appears in a person, and Isaiah 53:1 asks to whom it has been revealed. The correspondence is strongest as a contrast: the arm that could not be bound is replaced by the arm that brings salvation by being pierced, Isaiah 53:5.

typology.type: Babylon as God's sword in a pagan hand, Ezekiel 30:24 to 25
typology.fulfillment: God places His sword in the hand of a king who does not know Him. Isaiah 10:5 calls Assyria 'the rod of My anger,' and Jeremiah 51:20 calls Babylon His war club, and both are later judged. Pilate, who had power only 'from above,' John 19:11, and the rulers who crucified the Lord of glory, 1 Corinthians 2:8, belong to the same pattern: human agents who did what God's plan had determined, Acts 4:27 to 28, yet remained responsible. The type is limited in that Babylon is judged for its own pride, while Christ is the willing victim.

typology.type: The scattering of the Egyptians among the nations, Ezekiel 30:23 and 26
typology.fulfillment: The phrase repeated in verses 23 and 26 mirrors the scattering Israel suffered, and so Egypt is brought low by the same experience of dispersion. Later, the gospel gathers the scattered of every nation, as at Pentecost, when Egypt and Libya are named among the lands represented, Acts 2:10. The type is a negative one: scattering is judgment, and its reversal is the gathering of the church, John 11:52.

study.christ:
This chapter does not mention a Messiah, and the connections to Christ are better built from the arm and the day than from anything in the story of Egypt.

The arm is the strongest thread. In Ezekiel 30 the arm of Pharaoh, the arm of flesh, is set against the arm of God, who 'will strengthen the arms of Babylon's king' and decide the war. The prophets carried the image forward. Isaiah 51:9 cries, 'put on strength, O arm of the LORD,' remembering how it cut Rahab to pieces, and Isaiah 52:10 says that the LORD 'has bared His holy arm in the sight of all the nations.' Then Isaiah 53:1 asks, 'to whom has the arm of the LORD been revealed?' and goes on to describe a suffering servant. John quotes that verse when people did not believe in Jesus despite His signs, John 12:37 to 38, and so the Gospel itself identifies Jesus as that arm. The arm that was bared in Egypt's history is revealed in a man whose own arms were nailed open.

The contrast is instructive. Pharaoh's arm was broken and unbound, and it never held the sword again. The arm of the Lord was pierced and bound in grave clothes, and rose. Where Egypt's strength could not be mended, the One who was wounded for our transgressions, Isaiah 53:5, was raised, and by His raising He is declared to be the Son of God with power, Romans 1:4.

The day is the second thread. Ezekiel's day of clouds is the warning that the nations will give account. The New Testament pictures the Day of the Lord as a judgment overseen by Christ, Acts 17:31, and the darkness at His crucifixion, Matthew 27:45, places the first stroke of that day on Him. Those who have trusted in an arm of flesh will meet the day without cover; those who have trusted in Him find that He has already stood under it.

A word of care is needed. Ezekiel's oracle is not a hidden prophecy of the crucifixion. It is a plain oracle of judgment on Egypt, and the Christ-ward reading depends on the way Isaiah and the Gospels pick up its vocabulary. It is the shared language of arm, day and yoke that makes the connection, not a coded detail in the history of Pharaoh's army.
study.god:
God appears here as the one who sets the calendar. The first line fixes 'the day,' 'near,' and the second oracle opens with a specific date, so the God of Ezekiel is not the god of an eternal, timeless idea but the Lord who acts on particular days. The dates, the cities and the border markers are an assertion that He is Lord of the map and the calendar as well.

He is sovereign over alliances. Verses 5 and 6 show that no coalition can hide a proud power, and verse 9 shows that even Cush, far to the south, is shaken by messengers 'from Me.' God sends messengers, in ships, to a land that did not expect them. He reaches to nations that do not know Him.

He is the God who both breaks and strengthens, and notice the repeated personal verbs: 'I have broken,' 'I will break,' 'I will strengthen,' 'I will place My sword.' Babylon is not an independent actor. The text refuses to let Nebuchadnezzar's victory be a human accomplishment, which is the same refusal Pharaoh's boast in chapter 29 had made impossible. And when Babylon is the strong one, it is only because God has put the sword in its hand, which tells later readers that Babylon's turn will come.

He is also a God who does not treat idols as neutral. Verse 13 says, 'I will destroy the idols and put an end to the images in Memphis.' The gods of Egypt, which in Jeremiah 43:12 are burned and taken captive, are exposed as powerless. The judgment is therefore also a lesson about worship.

To see this is to be freed from two fears. One is fear of the empire that seems to control everything. The other is the fear that God's silence means indifference. The oracle says that God is exact, dated, and active, and that He will be known. For worship this means praise for a God whose arm is never broken, and humility before a God who can break any other.

crossReferences.note: Isaiah's burden against Egypt says the LORD rides on a swift cloud and that Egypt's idols will tremble. It is the earlier prophetic prototype for Ezekiel's day of clouds and the destruction of idols in Memphis in verse 13.

The LORD will punish Amon of Thebes, Pharaoh, Egypt with her gods and those who trust in Pharaoh, and then Egypt will be inhabited again. This matches the targeting of Thebes in Ezekiel 30:14 and 15 and the focus on those who trust in Egypt.

Neco's army was defeated at Carchemish by Nebuchadnezzar in the fourth year of Jehoiakim. This is the best candidate for the earlier break of Pharaoh's arm in Ezekiel 30:21 and 22, and it anchors the image in history.

Pharaoh's army marched out to help Jerusalem, and the Babylonians withdrew for a time. Jeremiah says the army will go home and the city will fall. It is the likely backdrop to the dated oracle in Ezekiel 30:20 about the arm that cannot be bound for healing.

Nebuchadnezzar will burn the temples of Egypt's gods and wrap himself with the land as a shepherd with his garment. It shows the destruction of Egypt's idols promised in Ezekiel 30:13 and the speed and ease of Babylon's campaign.

The great Day of the LORD is near, with a vocabulary of wrath, darkness and 'clouds and blackness.' Ezekiel 30:3 uses the same phrase as part of a day of judgment for the nations, which shows that the prophets drew on a common tradition.

The Day of the LORD is near for all the nations, and as they have done it will be done to them. It is a one verse summary of what Ezekiel 30 says in its focus on Egypt and her allies, and it shows the principle behind the sentence.

The prophet calls the arm of the LORD to awake as in the days when it cut Rahab to pieces and dried up the sea for the redeemed. It reads the arm as the agent of both judgment and rescue, which is the double work the arm does in Ezekiel 30.

Isaiah asks to whom the arm of the LORD has been revealed. Set beside Pharaoh's arm in Ezekiel 30, the question points to a different kind of strength, which the Gospel of John applies to Jesus in John 12:37 to 38.

Israel's shepherds are charged with not having bound up the injured. The same verb of binding up is used of the arm of Pharaoh in Ezekiel 30:21, so the book links a failed shepherd and a failed king as figures who cannot heal.

Multitudes in the valley of decision, with the Day of the LORD near. It places the Day of the LORD in a setting of the nations gathered for judgment, which widens the scope of Ezekiel's day of clouds beyond Egypt.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's story begins with a God who creates and humans who must trust His word, and it quickly becomes a story of people looking for strength elsewhere. The fall in Genesis 3 is that move: to take what appears strong and desirable and to rely on it. Ezekiel 30 shows the pattern at the level of nations. Egypt is the oldest place where strength was organised into an empire, and Judah's repeated flight to her is the repeated fall.

In the story of redemption Egypt is both the house of slavery and the place where God first shows what His arm can do. 'I will redeem you with an outstretched arm,' He says in Exodus 6:6. Ezekiel 30 turns that arm, the arm that once freed Israel, toward Egypt's own allies, and it shows that God's way of dealing with the nations is consistent from the first chapters of Exodus to the last of the prophets. The day of clouds is the same God, with the same arm.

What the chapter sets up is a larger day. The prophets' repeated phrase, 'the Day of the LORD,' becomes in the New Testament the great day on which Christ will judge the world, Acts 17:31, and the arm of the LORD is revealed in Jesus. The darkness of Ezekiel 30:3 and 18 finds its centre at the cross, Matthew 27:45, where the day of judgment fell on the Son so that others could pass through it.

The story ends with a restoration that includes Egypt. Isaiah 19:25 says 'Blessed be Egypt My people,' and Psalm 68:31 says that Cush will stretch out her hands to God. The first Gentile convert named in Acts is an Ethiopian official, Acts 8:27. In the end, the allies and cities in Ezekiel's list are among the nations who bring their glory into the city of God, Revelation 21:24. The day that brought them down is the same day that makes room for them.

quiz.q: Which nations are named as falling alongside Egypt in this chapter's opening oracle?

options.text: Cush, Put, Lud, Libya, and the men of the covenant land.
options.note: Verse 5 names exactly these allied peoples falling with Egypt by the sword.

options.text: Only Israel and Judah.
options.note: Israel and Judah are not the nations named as falling with Egypt here; the allies named are Cush, Put, Lud, and Libya.

options.text: Assyria and Persia alone.
options.note: Neither is named specifically in this chapter's list of Egypt's falling allies.

options.text: Only the Philistines.
options.note: The Philistines are not the allies named in this passage; the text specifies Cush, Put, Lud, and Libya.

quiz.q: What phrase does the LORD use in verse 3 to describe the coming judgment on Egypt and the nations?

options.text: The Day of the LORD, a day of clouds and a time of doom for the nations.
options.note: Verse 3 uses this exact phrase, language elsewhere often tied to Israel's own accountability but here applied to the nations broadly.

options.text: The year of Jubilee.
options.note: Jubilee is a term for release and restoration, the opposite of the judgment language used in this verse.

options.text: The feast of harvest.
options.note: Not the phrase used; verse 3 speaks of judgment and doom, not a harvest festival.

options.text: The season of exile alone, without further explanation.
options.note: The specific, weighty phrase used is 'the Day of the LORD,' not simply 'exile.'

quiz.q: What happens to the idols and images of Memphis, according to verse 13?

options.text: The LORD declares He will destroy them and put an end to them, along with removing any prince from Egypt.
options.note: Verse 13 states this directly regarding Memphis's idols and Egypt's princely rule.

options.text: They are moved safely to Thebes for protection.
options.note: No such relocation is described; the text describes destruction, not preservation elsewhere.

options.text: They are left untouched while only the city walls are destroyed.
options.note: The text specifically targets the idols and images themselves for destruction, not merely the walls.

options.text: They are given to Babylon as tribute rather than destroyed.
options.note: The text describes destruction of the idols, not their transfer as tribute.

quiz.q: What does the image of Pharaoh's broken arm, verses 20 to 22, communicate?

options.text: That Pharaoh's military strength is already broken beyond any human power to heal, and God will break it further.
options.note: Verses 21 to 22 explicitly describe the arm as unhealed and unsplinted, soon to be broken entirely.

options.text: That Pharaoh had suffered a literal accidental injury unrelated to any battle.
options.note: The 'arm' functions as a symbol of military and political strength throughout Scripture, not merely a literal medical case.

options.text: That Pharaoh's strength was actually growing stronger during this period.
options.note: The opposite is described; his strength, pictured as a broken arm, is declared already failing and beyond repair.

options.text: That Egypt's economy alone was affected, with no impact on her military power.
options.note: The 'arm' image specifically points to strength to 'hold the sword,' a clearly military meaning, not merely economic.

quiz.q: Whose arm does the LORD say He will strengthen in place of Pharaoh's?

options.text: The arms of the king of Babylon, placing His own sword in that king's hand.
options.note: Verses 24 to 25 state this explicitly, contrasting Babylon's strengthened arm with Pharaoh's broken one.

options.text: The arms of the Egyptian priesthood.
options.note: Not mentioned in this passage; the strengthened arm belongs to Babylon's king, not Egyptian priests.

options.text: The arms of Israel's own king.
options.note: Israel's king is not named here as the beneficiary; the text specifies Babylon's king receiving strengthened arms.

options.text: No one; both Egypt's and Babylon's strength are said to fail equally.
options.note: The text draws a clear contrast, Babylon's arms strengthened, Pharaoh's broken, not an equal failure of both.

questions: This chapter applies the weighty phrase 'the Day of the LORD' to Egypt, a nation outside God's covenant with Israel. Where do you need to remember that God's standards of justice and accountability apply universally, not only to people who claim to follow Him?

City after city in Egypt is named individually in this judgment; nothing is too specific or too distant for God's attention. Is there an area of your own life you assume is too small or too hidden for God to be concerned with?
Pharaoh's arm is described as already broken, beyond human power to splint or heal. What strength or ability are you leaning on that may already be failing, whether you have noticed it yet or not?

God strengthens Babylon's arm, a pagan king's, for His own purposes, even though Babylon does not know Him. Where have you seen God use unexpected people or circumstances, even ones that seemed opposed to your good, to accomplish something of His purpose in your life?

Isaiah later asks, 'to whom has the arm of the LORD been revealed,' a question answered in Christ's unbreakable strength. Where in your life this week do you need to lean on the arm of the LORD rather than your own arm of flesh?

translationNotes.note: The phrase 'men of the covenant land' likely refers to Jewish mercenaries or settlers known to have lived in Egypt during this period, rather than to Israel or Judah as a whole nation.

Zoan, Thebes, Pelusium, On, Pi-beseth, and Tahpanhes are all identifiable major cities across the length of Egypt, from the Nile delta in the north to Upper Egypt in the south, showing the judgment described reaches the entire land, not one region alone.

The image of an unhealed, unsplinted arm assumes the ancient practice of binding a broken limb with a bandage or splint for it to mend properly; the text specifies this normal remedy has not been applied, meaning the injury is left to worsen rather than heal.
